summary: Act on a 3rd-party review: (1) pin the Luau target (commit/tag, surface, vector width, flags, oracle, integer-constant question); (2) verify+correct the conformance table against a REAL reference-Luau binary (resolve the named contradictions + spot-check high-risk rows + define the test-backed method); (3) Wasm 3.0 impact on locked decisions; (4) broad benchmark suite vs reference Luau + a reference baseline; then synthesize a point-by-point response

result.summary: PINNED LUAU TARGET SPEC (addresses [C1]). Recommendation: pin the conformance target to Luau release tag 0.709 (commit b968ef742741bb2b703afc3b3c53f06608c87481, released 2026-02-21), because that is EXACTLY what our local oracle builds: mlua 0.11.6 -> mlua-sys 0.10.0 -> luau0-src 0.18.3+luau709. Pinning the spec to the oracle eliminates the oracle-vs-target drift that is the root cause of the [C2] conformance-table contradictions. Surface = standalone luau.org language + stdlib (base/coroutine/table/os/string/math/debug/utf8/bit32/buffer/vector), explicitly NOT the Roblox engine API. Vector width = 3 f32 (LUA_VECTOR_SIZE default 3; mlua luau-vector4 NOT enabled). FFlags = compiled defaults, override NONE; the only 3 script-visible VM FFlags at 0.709 (LuauStacklessPcall, UseNewTraceback, LuauMathSeedEncode) all default FALSE and our oracle leaves them off. CRITICAL RESOLUTION on integers: integers are NOT script-visible in the pinned target; f64/IEEE-754 double is the only script-level number type, so 50-conformance "f64-only" is CORRECT. The reviewer correctly spotted int64 LUA_TINTEGER and LBC_CONSTANT_INTEGER in CURRENT (0.727) source, but these are an in-development, default-OFF feature gated by FFlag::LuauIntegerType2=false requiring new `i`-suffix literals and bytecode v8 (default compile target is v7); 0.709 has none of that machinery at all.

findings.topic: Local oracle identity (the answer to sub-question e)
findings.finding: The spike's oracle chain is mlua 0.11.6 (checksum ccd36acf...) -> mlua-sys 0.10.0 -> luau0-src 0.18.3+luau709 (checksum e73f7d752741...). The '+luau709' build metadata means it vendors and compiles upstream Luau release 0.709. So mlua 0.11 vendors Luau 0.709. Spike features are only ["luau","vendored"]: luau-codegen, luau-vector4, and any set_fflag calls are NOT used, so the oracle runs Luau's compiled defaults.

Pin to tag 0.709, commit b968ef742741bb2b703afc3b3c53f06608c87481 (lightweight tag, released 2026-02-21). Rationale: it is bit-identical to what the local oracle builds, so spec==oracle (kills C2 drift); mlua 0.11 is the chosen embedding runtime and cannot run a Luau newer than it vendors; the 50-conformance table is already '709-row' aligned. Tradeoff: 0.709 is ~18 weekly releases behind HEAD (0.727, 2026-06-26). Policy: re-pin only when mlua bumps its vendored Luau, re-running the full conformance suite at each bump.

Surface = standalone luau.org language + stdlib as registered in linit.cpp at 0.709: base (globals), coroutine, table, os, string, math, debug, utf8, bit32, buffer, and a vector library (luaopen_vector / LUA_VECLIBNAME). Explicitly EXCLUDE the Roblox engine API: no game/workspace/script globals, no Roblox Instance/DataModel, no Roblox task scheduler, no Roblox-specific typeof extensions. require()/file resolution is host policy (sandbox or exclude), not part of the language conformance surface.

Standalone Luau defaults LUA_VECTOR_SIZE to 3 (luaconf.h: '#define LUA_VECTOR_SIZE 3 // must be 3 or 4', with LUA_EXTRA_SIZE = LUA_VECTOR_SIZE-2). The TValue union physically stores float v[2] with the 3rd lane in TValue::extra. mlua exposes a luau-vector4 feature to switch to 4, but the spike does NOT enable it. PIN: vector width = 3 script-visible f32 lanes. Note bytecode also carries LBC_CONSTANT_VECTOR and there is a native LUA_TVECTOR value type.

findings.topic: FFlags in the pinned target (sub-question d)
findings.finding: Pin = compiled defaults, override nothing. The macro LUAU_FASTFLAGVARIABLE(flag) defaults to false (Common.h: FValue<bool> flag(#flag,false,false)). The complete set of script-visible-semantics FFlags referenced in the 0.709 VM is exactly three, all default FALSE: LuauStacklessPcall (pcall/xpcall impl + yield/error edge behavior), UseNewTraceback (debug.traceback string format), LuauMathSeedEncode (default seed of unseeded math.random; irrelevant since we always seed explicitly in the determinism profile). The standalone luau CLI and mlua do not flip these, so oracle behavior == flags-off behavior. rustia should replicate the flags-off semantics.

findings.topic: CRITICAL: integers are NOT script-visible at 0.709 (source evidence)
findings.finding: Luau 0.709 has no integer machinery: the only numeric value tag is LUA_TNUMBER (no LUA_TINTEGER in lua.h's lua_Type enum); the TValue union stores 'double n' for numbers, 'int b' for bool, 'float v[2]' for vectors -- no integer slot; bytecode constant kinds are NIL/BOOLEAN/NUMBER/STRING/IMPORT/TABLE/CLOSURE/VECTOR -- there is NO LBC_CONSTANT_INTEGER. lua_Number=double; lua_Integer=int and lua_Unsigned=unsigned are C-API-only typedefs used by lua_pushinteger/luaL_checkinteger/bit32/buffer for boundary conversion -- not a value type. LOP_LOADN carries a 16-bit signed immediate (-32768..32767) but executes setnvalue() -> stores a DOUBLE; that codegen/encoding optimization is the 'bytecode integer' a reader can mistake for a script type.

findings.topic: CRITICAL: integers NOT script-visible -- running-oracle proof
findings.finding: Ran probes through the mlua/Luau-0.709 oracle: type(3)=type(3.0)=type(7//2)=type(0x10)=type(bit32.bor(1,2))=type(math.floor(3.7))=type(buffer.readi32(...)) all == 'number'. math.type == nil (Lua 5.3's integer/float discriminator is deliberately ABSENT in Luau). 3==3.0 -> true. Decisive precision test: 9007199254740993 (2^53+1) prints 9007199254740992 and 2^63 prints 9223372036854776000 -- i.e. values round to nearest double, which is impossible if a script-visible int64 existed. tostring(3)==tostring(3.0)=='3' (Luau prints integer-valued doubles with %.14g). Conclusion: f64 is the only script-level number type; 50-conformance 'f64-only' is CORRECT for the pinned target.

findings.topic: CRITICAL: the reviewer's int64/LBC_CONSTANT_INTEGER sighting is a default-OFF, in-flight feature in CURRENT (0.727) source
findings.finding: At HEAD/0.727 the reviewer is literally right that the source contains them, but they are gated off: lua_Type adds LUA_TINTEGER (and experimental LUA_TCLASS/LUA_TOBJECT); the TValue union gains 'int64_t l' with ttisinteger/setivalue; Bytecode.h adds LBC_CONSTANT_INTEGER (bytecode 'Version 8: ... Currently supported') and a typename 'integer'. BUT: (1) emission and the new `i`-suffix integer literal (e.g. 1000000000i, see Compiler.cpp 'like -1000000000i' and Parser.cpp scratchData.back()=='i') are gated behind FFlag::LuauIntegerType2, which is LUAU_FASTFLAGVARIABLE -> default FALSE; (2) the compiler's default bytecode target is LBC_VERSION_TARGET=7, below the v8 required for integer constants; (3) classes are gated by FFlag::DebugLuauUserDefinedClassesRuntime (Debug-prefixed = experimental, default false). So with default flags even on 0.727, plain `3` compiles to LBC_CONSTANT_NUMBER (double) and type(3)=='number'. The exact governing FFlag is LuauIntegerType2 (default false).

Primary oracle: the existing spike (mlua 0.11.6, vendored Luau 0.709) -- already builds+runs on aarch64-mac, no extra toolchain. Secondary cross-check oracle: build the standalone luau CLI from luau-lang/luau at tag 0.709 via cmake for a canonical (non-mlua) reference, useful to confirm mlua doesn't perturb defaults. Reproducibility anchors to cite in 00-constraints: Luau tag 0.709 / commit b968ef742741bb2b703afc3b3c53f06608c87481; luau0-src 0.18.3+luau709 checksum e73f7d752fe2ef0a41f132b83d0be154c6ae0ed84967b4df80a16901866be075; mlua 0.11.6; mlua-sys 0.10.0.

luau-lang/luau latest release at investigation time is 0.727 (published 2026-06-26); tags descend 0.727,0.726,...; 0.709 was 2026-02-21. So pinning 0.709 deliberately trades currency for oracle-fidelity. The 0.709->0.727 deltas most relevant to a future 'full parity' bump are the default-off LuauIntegerType2 (integer type) and user-defined Classes -- neither changes f64-only conformance today.

corrections_or_decisions: 00-constraints C1: replace 'latest Luau' with a hard pin: target = Luau tag 0.709, commit b968ef742741bb2b703afc3b3c53f06608c87481 (2026-02-21), reproduced by luau0-src 0.18.3+luau709 via mlua 0.11.6 / mlua-sys 0.10.0. State re-pin policy: only move when mlua bumps its vendored Luau, and re-run the full conformance suite at each bump.

00-constraints / spec: record SURFACE = standalone luau.org language + stdlib {base, coroutine, table, os, string, math, debug, utf8, bit32, buffer, vector}; explicitly NOT Roblox engine API (no game/workspace/script/Instance/DataModel/Roblox task). require/module resolution is host policy, out of the conformance surface.
Spec: VECTOR width = 3 script-visible f32 lanes (LUA_VECTOR_SIZE=3 default; do NOT enable mlua's luau-vector4). Native LUA_TVECTOR value type + LBC_CONSTANT_VECTOR + vector stdlib are in-scope.

Spec: FFlags = compiled defaults, override none. Document that the three script-visible VM flags at 0.709 (LuauStacklessPcall, UseNewTraceback, LuauMathSeedEncode) are all default-false and rustia targets flags-off semantics. Never depend on unseeded math.random.

50-conformance: KEEP 'f64-only' -- it is CORRECT for the pinned target. RESOLVE/DOWNGRADE the 'integer subtype' open decision: there is no script-visible integer in Luau 0.709, and even at HEAD (0.727) integers are default-OFF behind FFlag::LuauIntegerType2 (=false) requiring new `i`-suffix literals + bytecode v8 (default target v7). Reframe it as a WATCH item: revisit f64-only only if/when LuauIntegerType2 flips to default-true upstream.

50-conformance: add a note distinguishing three things commonly conflated as 'integers' that remain pure f64/double at script level: LOP_LOADN's 16-bit immediate (codegen), lua_Integer/lua_Unsigned C-API typedefs (boundary conversion only), and bit32/buffer integer semantics (operate on doubles reinterpreted as uint32 / read back as doubles). Cite math.type==nil as the canonical proof Luau has no integer subtype.

Process: re-derive the entire 50-conformance table by running each row against the 0.709 oracle (spike), since the pin now makes spec==oracle; this is the mechanism to clear the remaining [C2] contradictions (table.maxn/foreach, math.map, pairs/__iter, getfenv/setfenv).

result.summary: Built the broad benchmark suite for [H2] at <agent-workdir> (11 representative .luau workloads + a Rust mlua harness) and ran the first-cut REFERENCE-LUAU native baseline that the public "faster than reference Luau / ~5x koto" claim must beat. Also ported the feasible subset to koto 0.16.1 and ran a koto baseline so the per-workload koto multiplier is real, not assumed. This measures THE BAR, not rustia (no rustia engine exists yet). Oracle: Luau 0.709 (luau0-src 0.18.3+luau709 via mlua 0.11.6, luau+vendored), koto 0.16.1, aarch64-mac, --release/LTO/single-thread. Net result: reference Luau is ~4.7x-9x faster than koto on most workloads (so matching Luau roughly delivers the ~5x-koto claim), with two important exceptions — generic_iteration is at PARITY (koto ~1.0x) and pcall/try-catch where koto is actually faster — meaning the blanket "~5x koto" claim is NOT uniform and must be stated per-workload.

findings.topic: Reference-Luau native baseline (ns per unit, min of 9 reps)
findings.finding: dense_tables 9636.9 ns; sparse_tables 9165.2 ns; oop_metamethods 237.3 ns; closures_upvalues 21.7 ns; string_patterns 1000.6 ns; string_format 290.1 ns; coroutines 37.7 ns; pcall_xpcall 614.9 ns; generic_iteration 2067.5 ns; stdlib_math_table 88.7 ns; serialization 19410.0 ns. Each f(n) is one host->VM call doing n internal units, so FFI overhead is amortised to ~0 (pure in-VM throughput). Units differ per workload; compare rustia per-workload only.

findings.topic: koto 0.16.1 baseline + per-workload koto multiplier (koto_ns / luau_ns)
findings.finding: dense_tables koto 86655 ns = 9.0x slower than Luau; sparse_tables 47166 = 5.15x; closures_upvalues 103.0 = 4.74x; coroutines 180.5 = 4.79x; stdlib_math_table 530.2 = 5.98x; generic_iteration 2084 = 1.01x (PARITY); pcall/try-catch koto 143.6 = 0.23x (koto FASTER, but Luau unit does 2 protected calls vs koto 1, so ~2x koto-faster like-for-like). So 'faster than Luau' generally implies '~5x koto' EXCEPT generic iteration (parity) and protected calls (koto already wins).

findings.topic: koto cannot faithfully run all workloads
findings.finding: string_patterns has NO koto analog (koto has no Lua-pattern/regex engine) -> koto multiplier is undefined there; rustia's pattern-engine perf can only be benched vs Luau. oop_metamethods (koto @meta maps), string_format (koto "{}".format), and serialization (manual) ARE expressible in koto but were not ported to bound effort + because semantics diverge; only string_patterns is a true koto gap.

findings.topic: koto numbers are the FLOAT (determinism-unsafe) path
findings.finding: The koto baseline uses native i64/f64 (mirrors ai_bakeoff SCRIPT_FLOAT). grabby's DETERMINISTIC koto path routes Q16.16 through host fxmul/curve calls and is materially slower (ai_bakeoff comment: koto per-tick ~30-40x native). So for the Deterministic sim profile the real koto multiplier rustia faces is much larger than the 5-9x measured here on the float path.

These three allocate a fresh table (and strings) per unit, so a large fraction of the ns/unit is GC churn, not raw table-op cost. This is representative of real code but means rustia's gc-arena-on-instruction-counter design is squarely on the critical path for these workloads — they are the best stress test of the GC choice.

findings.topic: Cheapest wins / hottest paths for rustia
findings.finding: Absolute Luau cost is dominated by serialization (19.4us), dense (9.6us) and sparse (9.2us) tables; the fastcall/dispatch-bound workloads (closures 22ns, coroutines 38ns, stdlib math 89ns) are where Luau's bytecode+fastcall lowering is hardest to beat and where rustia's big-match/br_table dispatch must be competitive to claim 'faster than Luau'.

No working Luau-on-wasm harness exists in the tree (alt-luau-wasm is a trivial NATIVE mlua spike despite its name; mlua+vendored-luau does not build to wasm32-unknown-unknown without emscripten/wasi). Producing wasm numbers (and JSC/SpiderMonkey cross-engine) is the [H3] pre-lock gate, not cheap, and was deferred. Native bar is established here.

corrections_or_decisions: Pin the H2 oracle exactly as Luau 0.709 (luau0-src 0.18.3+luau709, mlua 0.11.6 luau+vendored) and koto 0.16.1 — these are what the baseline was measured against; any future rustia comparison must use the same Luau build.

State the public perf claim PER-WORKLOAD, not as a blanket '~5x koto': it holds (4.7x-9x) for tables/closures/coroutines/stdlib-math but FAILS for generic iteration (Luau~=koto, ~1.0x) and protected calls (koto already faster). Drop or heavily qualify the single-number '~5x koto' headline.

Separate two koto multipliers in the docs: the float-path multiplier measured here (~5-9x) and the DETERMINISTIC-path multiplier (host fxmul/curve, ~30-40x native per ai_bakeoff) — the sim's real incumbent is the deterministic path, so rustia's honest 'vs koto' story for the sim is the larger number.
Record that string_patterns has no koto analog: rustia's Lua-pattern-engine performance can only be claimed relative to reference Luau, never as a koto multiplier.

Treat the broad benchmark as a GATE artifact: re-run this exact suite against rustia when it boots and require beating the per-workload Luau ns/unit column (this README+harness is the regression harness).
Move wasm + cross-engine (JSC/SpiderMonkey, Wasm 3.0 features) benchmarking under [H3] as the pre-lock gate; the existing alt-luau-wasm dir is not a real wasm harness and should not be cited as one.

synth.pinned_target:
PIN: Luau tag 0.709, commit b968ef742741bb2b703afc3b3c53f06608c87481 (released 2026-02-21). This is bit-identical to what the local oracle builds (mlua 0.11.6 -> mlua-sys 0.10.0 -> luau0-src 0.18.3+luau709, checksum e73f7d752fe2ef0a41f132b83d0be154c6ae0ed84967b4df80a16901866be075), so SPEC == ORACLE, which is what kills the C2 drift. rustia is a from-scratch engine that TARGETS 0.709 semantics; it does NOT embed mlua — mlua/Luau-0.709 is only the conformance oracle vehicle.

SURFACE: standalone luau.org language + stdlib registered in linit.cpp at 0.709 = {base globals, coroutine, table, os, string, math, debug, utf8, bit32, buffer, vector}. Oracle-confirmed present: os/coroutine/debug/utf8/bit32/buffer/vector/table/string/math = table; io = nil, package = nil. Explicitly NOT the Roblox engine API (no game/workspace/script/Instance/DataModel/Roblox task scheduler/Roblox typeof extensions). require()/module resolution is HOST POLICY, outside the conformance surface.

VECTOR WIDTH: 3 script-visible f32 lanes (luaconf.h LUA_VECTOR_SIZE=3; LUA_EXTRA_SIZE=1). Do NOT enable mlua's luau-vector4 feature. Native LUA_TVECTOR + LBC_CONSTANT_VECTOR + the vector stdlib are in-scope.

FFLAGS: compiled defaults, override NONE. LUAU_FASTFLAGVARIABLE defaults to false. The only three script-visible-semantics VM flags at 0.709 (LuauStacklessPcall, UseNewTraceback, LuauMathSeedEncode) all default FALSE and the oracle leaves them off; rustia replicates flags-off semantics and never depends on unseeded math.random.

ORACLE: primary = the existing spike (mlua 0.11.6 vendored Luau 0.709, builds+runs on aarch64-mac, no extra toolchain). Secondary cross-check (recommended, to confirm mlua does not perturb defaults / sandbox state) = build the standalone luau CLI from luau-lang/luau at tag 0.709 via cmake.

INTEGER-VISIBILITY VERDICT: integers are NOT script-visible at 0.709 -> f64/IEEE-754 double is the only script-level number type, so 50-conformance's "f64-only" is CORRECT. Oracle proof (re-run by me): math.type == nil; type(3)=type(3.0)=type(7//2)=type(0x10)=type(2^53)=type(1//1)="number"; 3==3.0 -> true; 9007199254740993 prints 9007199254740992 and 2^63 prints 9223372036854776000 (rounds to nearest double -> impossible if a script-visible int64 existed). The reviewer's int64/LBC_CONSTANT_INTEGER sighting is real but is in CURRENT (0.727) source as a default-OFF, in-flight feature gated by FFlag::LuauIntegerType2 (=false), requiring new `i`-suffix literals and bytecode v8 while the default compile target is v7; 0.709 has none of that machinery. ACTION: keep f64-only; DOWNGRADE the "integer subtype" major-open-decision to a WATCH/tripwire that fires only if LuauIntegerType2 flips to default-true upstream.

RE-PIN POLICY: move the pin only when the oracle's vendored Luau bumps (or LuauIntegerType2 ships on by default); re-run the full conformance suite against the new oracle before adopting.

conformance_corrections.row: NEW row to ADD — proper tail calls
conformance_corrections.corrected: Luau does NOT guarantee proper tail-call elimination. Oracle: `local function rec(n) if n==0 then return 'done' end return rec(n-1) end; rec(200000)` -> stack overflow error. rustia must therefore NOT implement unbounded PTC frame reuse for `return f(x)`; its recursion cap should error like Luau. (Load-bearing for the Wasm-3.0 reasoning: language-level tail calls are NOT a Luau feature, so Wasm return_call is irrelevant to Luau semantics as well as to dispatch.)

wasm3_design_updates: SHIPPED WASM TAIL-CALLS DO NOT REOPEN THE DISPATCH DECISION — keep big-match->br_table. Spike B measured fn-pointer/call-threaded dispatch as 1.34-1.51x SLOWER than br_table in V8, with the cost being call_indirect's runtime type-check + table-bounds-check on EVERY opcode, not missing tail-call optimization. return_call/return_call_indirect (now shipped: V8 Chrome 112+, SpiderMonkey Firefox 121+, JSC Safari 18.2+, Wasmtime) only remove return/stack-growth overhead; they do NOT remove the per-opcode indirect type+bounds check that made threading lose. br_table is a single in-function branch with zero call overhead and better branch prediction, so the large Spike-B margin stands. VERDICT: the dispatch lock holds; add only a cheap confirmatory micro-bench at the P1 cross-engine gate.

TYPED FUNCTION REFERENCES / call_ref IS THE ONE TO ACTUALLY MICRO-BENCH (still expected to lose). call_ref skips call_indirect's runtime type-check (type is statically known via the typed funcref), so it is the strongest threaded-dispatch contender on Wasm 3.0 — but it retains the indirect-branch misprediction cost and the call/spill/reload of live interpreter state across the call boundary, which br_table avoids entirely. Prior strongly favors br_table; schedule a call_ref vs br_table micro-bench during the P1 JSC/SpiderMonkey/V8 measurement (cheap, low-risk) and only revisit if it unexpectedly beats br_table on a baseline-compiler tier.

WASM GC: REJECTED for the script heap. rustia keeps gc-arena on linear memory. WasmGC objects are not byte-addressable and have engine-defined layout, so (a) it forfeits the deterministic instruction-counter full-collect and host-columnar rollback design, and (b) GC behavior/layout is NOT guaranteed bit-identical across V8/JSC/SpiderMonkey — a direct determinism violation. Record WasmGC as explicitly considered-and-rejected in the risk register, with the determinism rationale.

RELAXED-SIMD: STAYS BANNED (reinforces axis E). Relaxed-SIMD permits FMA contraction and engine-dependent rounding -> nondeterministic across engines. The determinism build already denies +relaxed-simd/+fma/fast-math (improvement #5). Only FIXED-WIDTH deterministic SIMD (f32x4 for the vector library, the P4 runner-up) is permitted, and only where bit-identical across engines is proven.

MULTIPLE MEMORIES: optional, low-priority. Could place the immutable Arc-shared stdlib image (improvement #9) in a second linear memory separate from the per-VM mutable heap for isolation, but the benefit is marginal and it adds an engine-support matrix dependency. WATCH/optional; not on the lock path.

LANGUAGE-LEVEL TAIL CALLS ARE A NON-ISSUE: oracle confirms Luau does not guarantee proper tail calls (rec(200000) stack-overflows), so rustia's stackless trampoline + recursion cap already covers Luau semantics portably and needs no Wasm tail-call instruction for conformance.

PRE-LOCK GATE UNCHANGED: H3's core requirement — measure the value-layout + the br_table dispatch on JSC (Safari/iOS WKWebView) and SpiderMonkey (Firefox), not just V8 — REMAINS the pre-lock gate. The Wasm-3.0 pass does not relax it; it adds two cheap line items (call_ref micro-bench, confirm relaxed-simd/WasmGC stay off) to that same P1 cross-engine measurement.
synth.benchmark_plan:
SUITE (the regression/lock artifact at <agent-workdir> 11 representative .luau workloads + a Rust mlua harness, each f(n) doing n in-VM units (FFI amortised to ~0; compare rustia PER-WORKLOAD, never across workloads). Oracle pinned EXACTLY: Luau 0.709 (luau0-src 0.18.3+luau709 via mlua 0.11.6 luau+vendored) and koto 0.16.1 (features=[arc]); aarch64-mac, --release/opt-level=3/LTO=fat/codegen-units=1/single-thread. Workloads: dense_tables, sparse_tables, oop_metamethods, closures_upvalues, string_patterns, string_format, coroutines, pcall_xpcall, generic_iteration, stdlib_math_table, serialization.

REFERENCE-LUAU BASELINE (ns/unit, min of 9) — THE BAR rustia must beat: dense_tables 9636.9; sparse_tables 9165.2; oop_metamethods 237.3; closures_upvalues 21.7; string_patterns 1000.6; string_format 290.1; coroutines 37.7; pcall_xpcall 614.9; generic_iteration 2067.5; stdlib_math_table 88.7; serialization 19410.0. koto multipliers (koto_ns/luau_ns): dense 9.0x, sparse 5.15x, closures 4.74x, coroutines 4.79x, stdlib_math 5.98x, generic_iteration 1.01x (PARITY), pcall 0.23x (koto FASTER; ~2x like-for-like since the Luau unit runs 2 protected calls vs koto's 1). string_patterns has NO koto analog (no Lua-pattern engine) -> can only be claimed vs Luau. dense/sparse/serialization are allocation+GC-dominated -> the best stress test of the gc-arena-on-instruction-counter choice. The dispatch/fastcall-bound leaves (closures 22ns, coroutines 38ns, stdlib_math 89ns) are where Luau's bytecode+FASTCALL lowering is hardest to beat and where br_table dispatch must be competitive to claim Luau-parity.

HONEST HEADLINE rustia should publish: DROP the single-number "~5x koto." Public claim = "at/near reference-Luau parity, validated per-workload across a broad 11-workload suite." Against koto this is ~5-9x on tables/closures/coroutines/stdlib-math, but only ~PARITY on generic iteration and a DEFICIT on protected calls (koto ~2x faster like-for-like) — so generic_iteration and pcall/xpcall are the two workloads rustia must at least MATCH Luau on or it visibly regresses vs koto. Two koto multipliers must be stated separately: the float-path (~5-9x, measured here) and the sim's REAL incumbent, koto's DETERMINISTIC path (host fxmul/curve, ~30-40x native per ai_bakeoff) — the latter is rustia's honest, larger win for grabby. The ~25x figure is the bespoke private-fork fused op (OP_UTIL), NOT a general/public claim.

PLAN / GATE ACTIONS: (1) treat the suite as a continuous gate — re-run vs rustia when it boots; require beating each per-workload Luau ns/unit column. (2) Build the still-missing Luau-on-wasm harness (emscripten or wasm32-wasi build of luau-lang/luau; the existing alt-luau-wasm dir is a NATIVE mlua spike, not a wasm harness — do not cite it) and run the same suite under node/V8 + JSC + SpiderMonkey: this IS the H3 pre-lock gate. (3) Add a realistic-FFI variant (many small host<->VM calls, the grabby KotoSelector shape) to complement the amortised-FFI design. (4) Add the deterministic-koto path (host fxmul/curve) to the koto harness for the true sim multiplier. (5) Replace min-of-N with criterion-style CIs. (6) Resolve the koto closures_upvalues semantics anomaly (probe returned 15,15 not 15,20) before trusting that checksum.

Drop the blanket '~5x koto'; publish 'at/near reference-Luau parity, per-workload' on the 11-workload suite. Wire the suite as a CI gate; wasm/cross-engine numbers are deferred to the H3 gate, not part of the native headline.

Cross-engine wasm (JSC + SpiderMonkey, not just V8) STAYS the pre-lock gate. Wasm-3.0 pass: shipped tail-calls do NOT reopen dispatch (br_table stays) — call_indirect type/bounds check, not missing TCO, was the threading killer; call_ref is the only contender, scheduled as a cheap P1 micro-bench expected to lose. WasmGC rejected (determinism/layout). Relaxed-SIMD stays banned; only deterministic f32x4 allowed. Build a real luau-on-wasm harness for the gate (alt-luau-wasm is not one).

Keep the two BUILT runtime profiles (Standard, Deterministic) from one codebase, surfaced under three NAMES. DeterministicSim is worth BUILDING (a genuine profile: capability-removal + frozen base tables enabling compile-time FASTCALL fold + instruction-count GC), NOT a config knob. ReproducibleStandard = Standard (public default). LuauCompat = the one to DEMOTE to config-knobs-over-Standard + a test posture, because true byte-parity with reference Luau on unspecified behavior (hash iteration order, transcendental ULPs from the system libm) is unachievable/undesirable without surrendering the determinism wins; offer a few knobs (e.g. reference-style NaN sign, unpinned iteration order) rather than a third engine build.

Two GC policies, one gc-arena collector. Standard/ReproducibleStandard: INCREMENTAL/paced collection driven by allocation debt (gc-arena Pacing) -> bounded pause times for console/mod/browser-frame VMs; GC timing script-invisible-but-not-bit-reproducible (fine for Standard; matches Luau's own incremental mark&sweep; write barrier already measured free at 3.18ns). Deterministic: keep FULL-collect-to-completion triggered ONLY by the instruction counter (never byte-debt; object sizes differ 32/64-bit), no observable partial state. Both produce identical script results; expose a pacing multiplier for Standard; version the Deterministic interval as part of the determinism ABI; tune both on realistic heap sizes at P1.

Promote both out of P4 runner-up status, but split the timing by dependency. HOT/COLD opcode split -> P1: structure the dispatch loop with a tight hot core (MOVE/LOADK/LOADN/GETTABLEKS/SETTABLEKS/CALL/RETURN/numeric-for/arith/GETIMPORT/FASTCALL/NAMECALL/cmp/jump) in the inner br_table and rare/edge ops out-of-line #[cold]; cheaper to design in than retrofit, and it directly de-risks the JSC/SpiderMonkey baseline-compiler tiers, so validate it via disassembly + the P1 cross-engine measurement (H3 gate). GETTABLEKS shape INLINE CACHE -> P2 (not P1): it depends on the dual-part table (#1) and string atom ids (#2) which ARE the P1 core; at P1 only RESERVE the aux/cache word in the bytecode layout and define a PER-VM IC side-table keyed by IP (never mutate the shared Arc<Program>; invalidate on shape change / safeenv deopt; charge the same logical-op fuel on hit or miss to keep the fuel ABI fusion-invariant), then implement+enable at P2.
